questions.question: What is Git and why is it called a distributed version control system?
questions.title: What Is Git?
questions.direct_answer: Git is a **distributed version control system** because each normal clone has its own repository database and can create commits, branches, diffs, and logs locally. Developers exchange commits through remotes, but no central server is required for local history operations. Shallow and partial clones are deliberate exceptions to a full local copy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the core architecture of Git and what 'distributed' means in practical terms beyond just buzzwords
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Git with GitHub or thinking distributed just means multiple people can use it — the key is that everyone has the full history locally
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain which operations are local, which exchange data with remotes, and why shallow or partial clones are an important boundary.

sections.title: Understanding Git as a Distributed VCS
sections.content:
Git tracks versions as a graph of commits. It is called **distributed** because a clone is a working repository with its own refs and object database, not merely a checkout that must ask one central server to create every revision. You can inspect history, make commits, create branches, and compare versions locally, then exchange objects and refs with one or more remotes.

A normal clone receives the history reachable through the refs selected by the clone. Git also supports shallow, single-branch, sparse, and partial clones, so “every clone contains every object and every branch” is not a reliable definition.

Distributed does not mean GitHub, cloud storage, or automatic backup. GitHub, GitLab, and other servers host repositories and collaboration features. A clone is useful redundancy for the history it actually has, but server policy, backups, and unpublished local work still matter.

sections.title: Setting Up and Using a Local Git Repository
When Git's Distributed Model Shines
sections.content: Use Git's distributed capabilities when **working remotely or with unreliable internet** — you can commit, branch, and review history during your commute or at a coffee shop with no WiFi. It's essential for **open-source projects** where hundreds of contributors fork the repository and work independently before submitting pull requests. In **enterprise Java projects**, even if you have stable network, the speed of local operations (viewing logs, creating branches, running diffs) makes daily development faster than centralized systems. The distributed model also provides **disaster recovery** — if your company's GitHub or GitLab server crashes, any developer can push their local copy to a new server and restore everything.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing Git with GitHub**: Git is the version control tool that runs on your machine; GitHub is just one hosting service for Git repositories (GitLab and Bitbucket are alternatives). Git existed years before GitHub.
- **Thinking distributed means cloud-based**: Distributed doesn't mean your code is in the cloud — it means every developer has a full copy locally. You can use Git without ever touching the internet.
- **Not understanding offline capability**: Freshers often think they need internet to commit or branch, so they wait to commit until they're online, leading to huge commits instead of small logical ones.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Git stores project history as commits in a local repository database.
- A normal clone can commit, branch, diff, and inspect history without a network connection.
- Remotes are used to exchange commits and refs; one central server is a convention, not a Git requirement.
- Shallow and partial clones may intentionally contain less history or fewer objects.
- Git is the VCS; GitHub and GitLab are hosting and collaboration services.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Git is a distributed version control system because each normal clone is a repository that can create and inspect history locally. I can commit, branch, view logs, or compare revisions without contacting GitHub. Later, `fetch`, `pull`, and `push` exchange objects and update refs with another repository called a remote.

For example, while offline I can create three commits on a feature branch. When the network returns, I fetch the team's work, integrate it according to the team policy, and push my branch. The remote is an important collaboration point, but it is not required for those local commits.

A useful boundary is that not every clone is a complete backup: Git supports shallow, single-branch, and partial clones, and local commits that were never pushed exist only in that repository. Distributed means repositories can hold and create history independently, not that every developer automatically possesses every possible object or that hosted backups are unnecessary.

questions.question: How does Git differ from SVN (Subversion)?
questions.title: Git vs SVN
questions.direct_answer: Git is distributed: commits and most history operations happen in a local repository and are later exchanged with remotes. Subversion is centralized: commits receive revisions from a central repository, although its working copy still supports several local operations. Both support branches; SVN commonly creates branches with cheap repository copies, while Git represents a branch as a ref to a commit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of architectural differences between distributed and centralized version control and their practical implications
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Just saying Git is modern and better without explaining concrete differences — always provide specific examples of how workflows differ
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that SVN's simpler permission model is why some large enterprises still use it for code with strict access control requirements

sections.title: Git vs SVN: Architectural Foundations
sections.content:
Git and Subversion both track versions, but they organize repositories differently. A Git clone is a local repository that can create commits and branches offline. An SVN working copy is connected to a central repository; publishing a commit creates a new repository revision on that server.

This does not mean every SVN command needs a network or that SVN branches copy every byte. SVN working copies can perform useful local operations, and `svn copy` within a repository is designed as a cheap copy. The important difference is the repository and commit model, not a claim that one tool is slow by definition.

Git identifies commits in a graph using object IDs and works naturally with many local branches and remotes. SVN uses central repository revision numbers and supports path-based authorization that some organizations value. The right comparison covers architecture, offline commits, identifiers, workflow, and administration rather than declaring one universally better.

sections.title: Git Is Local, SVN Needs the Server
sections.content:
```bash
# Git: create local history without contacting a remote
git switch -c feature
git commit -am "add feature"
git log --oneline
# Network is needed when exchanging work, for example:
git push origin feature

# Subversion: the commit is recorded in the central repository
svn commit -m "add feature"
# A repository-side SVN branch is commonly made with a cheap copy:
svn copy ^/trunk ^/branches/feature -m "create feature branch"
```

SVN's repository copy does not duplicate every file immediately; Git's branch is still a different and smaller concept—a movable ref in a commit graph.

sections.title: Choosing Between Git and SVN
sections.content:
Use **Git** for modern software projects where developers work remotely, need fast branching for feature development, and want the safety of distributed backups. It's the default choice for web applications, microservices, and open-source projects. Git shines when your team uses pull requests for code review.

Use **SVN** in legacy enterprise environments where strict path-based permissions are required (restricting access to specific folders within a repo), or when your team is already invested in SVN and migration costs outweigh benefits. Some large organizations use SVN for monolithic codebases where fine-grained access control to subsystems is critical. In practice, most Java freshers will only encounter Git, as SVN usage has declined significantly since 2010.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Saying Git is universally better**: While Git dominates today, SVN's simpler permission model genuinely matters in some contexts — blanket statements sound uninformed.
- **Not understanding the offline difference**: Freshers say Git is distributed but can't explain that in SVN you must be online to commit or view history, while Git lets you commit locally and sync later.
- **Thinking SVN branches are like Git branches**: In SVN, a branch is commonly a cheap repository path copy; in Git, a branch is a movable ref to a commit. This architectural difference fundamentally changes how teams use branching.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Git uses distributed repositories; SVN uses a central repository with client working copies.
- Git creates commits locally; an SVN commit is recorded by the central repository.
- A Git branch is a ref; an SVN branch is commonly a cheap repository path copy—not a full byte-for-byte copy.
- SVN has useful local working-copy operations, so it is wrong to say every SVN command needs the server.
- Choose using workflow, authorization, tooling, and migration needs rather than a universal winner.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The main difference is the repository model. Git is distributed, so a normal clone is a local repository: I can create commits and branches and inspect history offline, then exchange work with remotes. Subversion is centralized, so commits are created in the central repository and receive repository-wide revision numbers.

For example, on a train without network access I can run `git switch -c invoice-fix`, commit the fix, and inspect its history. I need the network only when I exchange that work with a remote. With SVN, I can edit and inspect parts of the working copy locally, but `svn commit` must contact the central repository to create a revision.

Their branch models also differ. A Git branch is a movable ref to a commit. In SVN, branches are usually directories created with `svn copy`, but that repository copy is cheap; it does not immediately duplicate every file. Therefore “SVN branches are slow full copies” is inaccurate.

SVN can also offer central path-based permissions that fit some organizations. Git is common for distributed collaboration and inexpensive local branching, but the good interview answer compares architecture, commit location, history identifiers, branching, and administration without saying one tool is always better.

questions.question: What are the three areas (or stages) in Git's local workflow?
questions.title: Git's Three Areas: Working Directory, Staging Area, Repository
questions.direct_answer: Git's local workflow is commonly explained with three areas: the **working tree** you edit, the **index** (staging area) that records the proposed next snapshot, and the **repository** that stores commits and other Git objects. `git add` updates the index; `git commit` creates a commit from the index.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Git's internal workflow model, which is fundamental to using commands like git add, git commit, git reset, and git stash correctly
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking git commit goes directly from working directory to repository, skipping the staging area — this misunderstanding causes confusion with commands like git add
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the staging area enables atomic logical commits by letting you commit only part of your changes, even from within a single file using git add -p

sections.title: Git's Three-Stage Architecture
sections.content:
Git organizes your work into three distinct areas, and understanding these is essential for using Git effectively. The **working directory** is simply the files and folders you see in your project — this is where you edit code in your IDE. When you save changes to a Java file, those changes exist only in the working directory. The **staging area** (also called the **index**) is a holding zone for changes you want to include in the next commit.

Think of it as a shopping cart: you select specific items (file changes) to purchase (commit) rather than buying everything in the store. You move changes from working directory to staging area with the git add command. The **local repository** is the repository storage in the hidden dot-git folder where Git saves committed snapshots. Once you run git commit, the staged changes become a new commit in repository history. This three-stage model is unique to Git — tools like SVN commit directly from working directory to server. The staging area might seem like extra complexity at first, but it gives you powerful control: you can stage only some files, or even specific lines within a file, enabling clean logical commits instead of messy everything commits.

sections.title: The Three Areas at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Working directory|~Files you edit|your project files in the IDE|changes start here|git status shows them as unstaged
amber|Staging area (index)|~The next commit, previewed|git add moves changes here|stage part of your work|enables clean, logical commits
emerald|Local repository|~The .git folder|git commit saves a snapshot|repository objects and refs|lives entirely offline
rose|The flow|~edit -> add -> commit|working -> staging -> repo|normal commits read their tree from the index|run git status to stay oriented

sections.title: Working with Git's Three Stages
When the Three-Stage Model Matters
sections.content:
The staging area becomes critical when **you've made multiple unrelated changes** and need to commit them as separate logical units. For example, you fixed a bug in OrderService and refactored formatting in three other files. Stage and commit the bug fix first, then stage and commit the refactoring — this keeps history clean.

Use the staging area for **partial commits during feature development**: you've added both the happy path and error handling, but error handling isn't done yet. Stage only the happy path files, commit them, and continue working on error handling. The staging area also enables **interactive staging** with git add -p (patch mode), where you can select specific code chunks within a file to stage, leaving other chunks unstaged. This is powerful when a single file has both completed and in-progress work.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using git commit -a blindly**: The dash-a flag stages all tracked files automatically, bypassing the staging area. Freshers use this to avoid typing git add, but it defeats the purpose of the three-stage model and leads to messy commits with unrelated changes.
- **Not understanding git reset**: Freshers think reset deletes changes, but git reset HEAD file just unstages a file, moving it from staging area back to working directory — the changes are still there.
- **Confusing staged with committed**: After git add, changes are staged but not recorded in a commit. You must still run git commit. If you switch branches without committing, staged changes come with you to the new branch.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Working tree**: checked-out files you edit.
- **Index/staging area**: the proposed snapshot for the next commit.
- **Repository**: commits, trees, blobs, and refs stored under the Git directory.
- `git add` copies selected content into the index; it does not move the working file.
- `git commit` creates a commit from the index; retention still depends on refs, reflogs, and garbage collection.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Git has three areas that changes flow through. First is the working directory, which is just the regular files and folders I see in my project. When I edit a Java file in IntelliJ and save it, that change exists in the working directory. Second is the staging area, which people also call the index. This is like a preparation zone for the next commit. When I run git add on a file, I'm copying that change from the working directory into the staging area. It's not committed yet, it's just marked as ready to commit. The third area is the local repository, which is the repository storage inside the hidden dot-git folder. When I run git commit, everything in the staging area gets saved as a snapshot in the repository. The key insight is that commits don't go directly from working directory to repository — they must pass through staging first. This might seem like extra work, but it gives you precise control. Let's say I've fixed a bug in OrderService and also refactored some formatting in three other files. I want those to be separate commits because they're unrelated changes. I can run git add OrderService.java to stage just the bug fix, commit it, then stage and commit the refactoring files separately. Without the staging area, I'd have to commit everything at once, which makes history messy. A common mistake freshers make is using git commit dash-a, which auto-stages all changes. That bypasses the whole point of the staging area and leads to kitchen-sink commits with unrelated stuff mixed together. Another mistake is thinking git add saves changes permanently — it doesn't. Add just stages them. You still need to commit. If you're ever confused about what's where, run git status. It clearly shows which files are in working directory only, which are staged, and which are committed.

questions.question: What is the difference between git init and git clone?
questions.title: git init vs git clone
questions.direct_answer: `git init` creates an empty Git repository in an existing or new directory. `git clone <url>` creates a new repository from another repository, configures a remote (normally named `origin`), fetches the selected history and refs, and usually checks out an initial branch. Clone options such as `--depth`, `--single-branch`, and `--filter` can intentionally limit what is copied.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic command knowledge and understanding when to use each — tests whether the candidate knows the typical workflows for starting vs joining projects
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using git init on a folder and then manually adding a remote when they should have just used git clone to pull down an existing GitHub repo
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that git clone automatically sets up remote tracking branches and configures your local main or master branch to track origin main

sections.title: git init vs git clone: Starting Points
sections.content:
Both commands create a Git repository, but they're used in completely different scenarios. **git init** initializes a brand new Git repository from scratch in your current directory. It creates the hidden dot-git folder with the necessary database structure, but the repository is empty — no commits, no branches yet. You use init when you're starting a new Java project on your laptop and want to add version control. After running init, you typically add files, make your first commit, and optionally connect to a remote repository later with git remote add. **git clone** copies an existing repository from a remote location (like GitHub, GitLab, or another developer's machine) to your local system. When you clone, you get the reachable history selected by the clone options. Git also automatically sets up a **remote** called origin pointing back to the source repository, and configures your local main branch to track the remote main branch. You use clone when joining an existing team project, contributing to open-source, or setting up the codebase on a new laptop.

For freshers, clone is by far the more common command because you're usually joining existing projects, not creating them.

sections.title: init vs clone in Commands
sections.content:
```bash
# git init — brand new empty repo; you wire up the remote yourself
git init                                   # creates .git, no commits yet
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git remote add origin https://github.com/me/new-project.git
git push -u origin main

# git clone — copy an existing repo; origin + tracking set up for you
git clone https://github.com/company/order-service.git
cd order-service
git remote -v        # origin is already configured
git pull             # works immediately, no setup needed
```

sections.title: Choosing Between init and clone
sections.content:
Use **git init** when you're creating a brand new Java project from scratch — maybe a personal learning project or a new microservice. Run it in your project folder after setting up the initial file structure. After the first commit, you can optionally push to GitHub by creating a repo there and running git remote add origin <url> followed by git push.

Use **git clone** when the repository already exists somewhere else. This is the typical scenario for freshers: your team lead sends you a GitHub URL, you run git clone https://github.com/company/order-service.git, and you get the entire codebase with history. Clone also works for setting up the same project on multiple machines — clone it on your work laptop, then clone again on your home desktop. One subtle point: if your company uses a repository template, you might clone that template and then remove the origin remote to start fresh.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using init when you should clone**: Freshers see a GitHub repo URL, run git init locally, copy files manually, and try to push — this creates a disconnected repo. Just git clone the URL instead.
- **Not understanding origin**: After git clone, freshers don't realize that origin is just a nickname for the remote URL. They think origin is a special Git keyword. It's just a conventional name that clone sets up for you.
- **Re-cloning unnecessarily**: If you accidentally delete your working directory files but the dot-git folder is intact, you don't need to re-clone. Just run git checkout to restore files. Cloning creates a new repository, which you don't need if you already have the Git history locally.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `git init` creates a repository without commits or a configured remote.
- `git clone` initializes a repository, fetches from another repository, and usually checks out an initial branch.
- Clone normally creates a remote named `origin`, though the name can be changed.
- The checked-out initial branch normally gets upstream configuration.
- Shallow, single-branch, no-tags, and partial clones are valid exceptions to 'all history and all objects'.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: git init and git clone both create a Git repository, but they're used in completely different situations. I'd use git init when I'm starting a brand new project from scratch on my local machine. Let's say I create a new Java project in IntelliJ for a personal learning exercise. I'd navigate to that project folder in the terminal and run git init. This creates the hidden dot-git folder, which is where Git stores all the repository data. At that point, the repository is empty — no commits yet, no branches. I'd then add my initial files and make my first commit. If I later want to push this to GitHub, I'd create a repo there, then run git remote add origin with the GitHub URL, and finally git push. On the other hand, git clone is what I'd use when I'm joining an existing project. This is way more common for freshers. My manager sends me a GitHub link to the team's order service repository. I run git clone followed by that URL, and Git downloads the entire repository to my machine — the history and remote-tracking refs selected by the clone. The clone command also does something smart: it automatically sets up a remote called origin that points back to the GitHub repo, and it configures my local main branch to track the remote main branch. That means I can just run git pull and git push without extra setup. One mistake I've seen is when people run git init for a project that already exists on GitHub. They think they need to init first and then connect it, but that's backwards. If the repo already exists remotely, just clone it. You only init when you're creating something brand new. Another thing to know is that git clone creates a subdirectory named after the repository. If I clone order-service, I'll get an order-service folder. I can customize that by adding a directory name at the end of the clone command. So to summarize: init is for starting a new project from zero, clone is for copying an existing repo. For most freshers, clone is what you'll use ninety percent of the time because you're joining teams and working on existing codebases.

questions.question: Is a Git commit a diff (set of changes) or a snapshot of the entire project?
questions.title: Git Commits Are Snapshots, Not Diffs
questions.direct_answer: Conceptually, a Git commit records a **snapshot**, not a line-by-line patch. The commit points to a root tree describing all tracked paths, and trees point to file-content blobs. Unchanged content can reuse the same objects; pack files may later use delta compression as a storage optimization without changing the snapshot model.

interviewer_intent.testing: Deep understanding of Git's data model — this separates candidates who've studied Git internals from those who only know surface commands
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying commits store only the changed lines like SVN does — this is backwards from how Git actually works and leads to misunderstanding commands like git checkout
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Git uses content-derived object IDs (SHA-1 or SHA-256, depending on repository format) and blob objects to store file contents, with trees linking blobs, and that Git packs files efficiently despite the snapshot model

sections.title: Git Commits as Snapshots, Not Diffs
sections.content:
This is one of Git's most misunderstood concepts. A **commit is a complete snapshot** of all tracked files at that point in time, not a delta or diff from the previous commit. When you commit, Git doesn't record that you changed line 42 in OrderService.java from X to Y. Instead, it captures the entire state of every tracked file. Each commit contains a **tree object** that lists every file and its content at that moment.

Think of it like taking a photo of your project — the photo shows everything, not just what changed since the last photo. This is fundamentally different from tools like SVN, which store commits as changesets (diffs applied to previous versions). Why does Git do this? Because snapshots make certain operations incredibly fast. When you run git checkout to switch to an old commit, Git just restores that snapshot directly — it doesn't have to replay hundreds of diffs. When you compare two commits, Git has both full states and can compute the diff on demand. Now, Git isn't wasteful — it uses **content-addressable storage** with content-derived object IDs. If a file doesn't change between commits, Git doesn't duplicate it; both commits point to the same stored content. Git also periodically packs objects to save space. But conceptually, every commit is a full snapshot.

sections.title: Visualizing Snapshots in Git History
Why Snapshots Matter in Practice
sections.content: Understanding snapshots helps when **checking out old code** — you're restoring a complete project state, not undoing changes one by one. This makes time travel fast and reliable. It's crucial for **branching decisions**: because commits are snapshots, creating a branch is just making a pointer to a commit, not copying files. The snapshot model also explains **why Git is fast at merging** — it compares three complete snapshots (your branch, target branch, and common ancestor) to determine conflicts, rather than replaying diffs. For **debugging with git bisect**, Git can jump directly to any commit snapshot to test if a bug exists, without reconstructing state from hundreds of deltas. Knowing this helps you **trust Git's integrity** — because commits are snapshots with content-derived object IDs, any corruption is immediately detected.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking commits store diffs**: This is how SVN works, not Git. In Git, diffs are computed on demand by comparing snapshots. Saying commits store diffs in an interview immediately reveals shallow Git knowledge.
- **Worrying about repository size**: Freshers think the snapshot model wastes space, but Git's content-addressable storage means unchanged files aren't duplicated. Git periodically packs objects efficiently.
- **Not understanding checkout behavior**: Because commits are snapshots, git checkout replaces your working directory with that snapshot — it's not replaying or undoing changes, it's swapping the entire state. This can be disorienting if you expect diff-based behavior.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- A commit points to a complete tree for the tracked project state.
- Trees describe directories; blobs store file content; commits connect snapshots into history.
- Unchanged files can reuse the same blob object across many commits.
- Pack files may delta-compress objects internally, but diffs are not the commit's logical data model.
- Repositories can use SHA-1 or SHA-256 object formats; object IDs should not be taught as universally SHA-1.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A Git commit is a snapshot of the entire project, not a diff. This trips up a lot of people because tools like SVN store commits as changesets — records of what lines changed. Git doesn't work that way. When I make a commit, Git captures the complete state of every tracked file at that moment. Each commit has a tree object that lists all the files and directories, and each file points to a blob object storing that file's content. It's like taking a photograph of the project. The photo shows everything, not just what's different from the last photo. Now, you might think this wastes a ton of space, but Git is smarter than that. It uses content-addressable storage with content-derived object IDs. If I commit and OrderService.java hasn't changed since the last commit, Git doesn't duplicate that file — both commits point to the same blob object. Git also runs garbage collection periodically, packing objects and compressing similar files to save space. But conceptually, every commit is a full snapshot. The reason Git does this is speed. When I run git checkout to go back to an old commit, Git just restores that snapshot directly. It doesn't have to replay a hundred diffs to reconstruct the old state. When I compare two commits with git diff, Git has both complete snapshots and computes the differences on the fly. This also makes branching super cheap — a branch is just a pointer to a commit snapshot, not a copy of files. A common mistake freshers make is saying commits store diffs because that's more intuitive from other version control systems. But in Git, diffs are derived by comparing snapshots, not stored directly. Understanding this helps you reason about commands like checkout and merge — they're manipulating snapshots, not replaying changes. It also explains why Git can detect file corruption so reliably — every commit's hash depends on the complete tree of file contents, so any bit flip breaks the hash chain immediately.
